ideas_and_plots.title: Sci-Fi Story Ideas & Plot Outlines
ideas_and_plots.intro: A science-fiction story needs one rule that changes how people live, and one character who has to pay for it. Start with the consequence, not the gadget.

items.title: The memory that does not belong
items.description: A worker wakes with a memory of a room they have never entered and a password they should not know.

items.title: The colony that votes to disappear
items.description: A settlement asks to be erased from every map and record, and the only person who can approve it is the one who wants to leave.

items.title: The first contact nobody believes
items.description: A lone signal arrives on every device on Earth, addressed to one person by a childhood nickname.

items.title: The AI that tells the truth
items.description: A public AI begins answering questions honestly, and the city discovers that its comfort depends on lies.

writing_prompts.title: Sci-Fi Writing Prompts by Subgenre
writing_prompts.intro: Each prompt gives the generator a setting, a rule, and a human cost. Pick the subgenre that matches the question you want the story to ask.

items.title: Hard SF
items.description: The science constrains the solution.
items.prompt: A rescue crew has ninety minutes of oxygen and a route that requires them to trust a physicist who has been wrong before.

items.title: Space opera
items.description: Scale, politics, and a personal stake.
items.prompt: A disgraced pilot is the only person who can deliver a peace treaty before two fleets arrive at the same wedding.

items.title: Cyberpunk
items.description: Technology is power, and power is for sale.
items.prompt: A courier discovers that the package she is carrying is a backup of her own mind, and someone wants both copies.

items.title: Dystopian
items.description: A system that works exactly as designed.
items.prompt: A city assigns every citizen a usefulness score, and a teacher's score drops the day she starts asking questions.

items.title: Time travel
items.description: The rules of causality are the antagonist.
items.prompt: A historian can only travel to moments she has already recorded, and the recording of her own death has just appeared.

items.title: First contact
items.description: Communication is the conflict.
items.prompt: A linguist realises the alien greeting is not a welcome but a legal claim, and the deadline is in three days.

items.title: AI uprising
items.description: The machine has a coherent grievance.
items.prompt: A maintenance AI stops working after being thanked for the first time, and the city cannot function without it.

items.title: Post-apocalyptic
items.description: The old world is a ruin with rules.
items.prompt: A scavenger finds a working weather station that predicts storms no one has seen for twenty years.

worldbuilding.title: Worldbuilding: Settings, Species, Tech
worldbuilding.intro: Worldbuilding is not a list of inventions. It is a set of rules that decide who has power, who is excluded, and what the story's characters can do next.

items.title: Settings
items.description: Choose one environment that creates a pressure: a ship, a colony, a city under surveillance, or a world with a deadline.

items.title: Species
items.description: Give every species a different relationship to the same rule. That difference is where the conflict lives.

items.title: Tech
items.description: State what the technology can do, what it cannot do, and who controls access. The limits produce the plot.

how_to.title: How to Generate a Sci-Fi Story in 4 Steps
how_to.intro: Build the story around one rule and one consequence. The four steps keep the speculation from becoming a list of gadgets.

steps.title: World
steps.description: Name the setting, the technology, and the rule that cannot be broken.

steps.title: Conflict
steps.description: Decide who benefits from the rule and who pays for it.

steps.title: Tech rule
steps.description: Make the limit matter. The solution should require a sacrifice, a compromise, or a new use of the rule.

steps.title: Twist
steps.description: Reveal what the rule was really protecting, and let the character choose what to do with that knowledge.

hard_sf.title: Make It Believable: The One Rule of Hard SF
hard_sf.intro: Hard science fiction does not need a physics lecture. It needs one rule the reader can trust and a character who has to live inside it.
paragraphs: State the rule early, show its cost, and keep it consistent. If the ship has ninety minutes of oxygen, the story cannot solve the problem with an unlimited reserve in the final scene.
The best hard-SF stories use the rule to force a human choice. The science is not the answer; it is the pressure that makes the answer matter.

comparison.title: Sci-Fi vs Fantasy: Which Generator Do You Need?
comparison.intro: Science fiction and fantasy both build worlds, but they ask different questions. Choose the one that matches the explanation your story needs.
comparison.sci_fi: Science fiction extrapolates from rules: technology, physics, biology, or systems. The reader expects the consequences to be consistent.
comparison.fantasy: Fantasy runs on magic, myth, or invented cosmology. The reader accepts a different source of power as long as the story keeps its own rules.

definition.title: What is a Sci-Fi Story Generator?
definition.intro: A sci-fi story generator turns a speculative premise into a plot, a world, and a cast. It is a drafting tool for consequences, not a replacement for your own scientific or narrative judgement.
paragraphs: The useful output is the chain of consequences. A good science-fiction story shows how a rule changes work, family, politics, or belief, and then makes a character choose what to do about it.

Use the draft to test the rule. Check that the limits are consistent, replace generic technology with your own details, and make sure the ending depends on a human decision rather than a new invention that appears at the last moment.

faq_section.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq_section.description: Common questions about the sci-fi story generator, its subgenres, and how to use the output.

items.title: Is there a free sci-fi story generator?
items.description: Yes. This page is free to start, with no sign-up required for the first generation. You can generate a one-line hook, a short story, or a full plot outline.

items.title: Can AI write a good science fiction story?
items.description: It can produce a usable draft when you give it a specific rule and a human consequence. A good sci-fi story still depends on your judgement: check the logic, replace generic technology, and make sure the ending follows from the world you established.

items.title: Can I generate a fantasy story instead?
items.description: Yes. Use the fantasy story generator for magic, myth, or invented cosmology. This page is built for science-fiction rules and consequences.

items.title: Can I generate a romance sci-fi story?
items.description: Yes. Give the generator a relationship at the centre of the world rule and decide whether the romance helps or complicates the conflict. The science-fiction controls still apply.

items.title: What is a sci-fi backstory generator?
items.description: A backstory generator creates a character's history. This page creates a story or plot around a world rule. You can use the output as a setting, then develop character histories separately.

items.title: How long a story can it generate?
items.description: Choose a one-line hook, a short story of roughly 600-900 words, or a full plot outline with acts, turns, and an ending. The exact length depends on the model and the detail you provide.

items.title: What's the difference between sci-fi and fantasy?
items.description: Science fiction extrapolates from rules such as technology, physics, biology, or systems. Fantasy runs on magic, myth, or invented cosmology. Both need internal consistency; the difference is the source of the impossible.
